title: Lester's hundred-choruses boast and learning from solo gigs in Minneapolis and Kansas City
summary: Lester said he could play a hundred different choruses, having stretched out with just rhythm in Minneapolis with Frank Hines in 1930-31 and at the Subway in Kansas City.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: When did he start saying that?
Oh, way back. He said, "I could play a hundred choruses, Phil, and play something different every chorus."
Do you remember when he first started to say that?
That was after he went to Kansas City. After he went up to Minneapolis, after I saw him. He said he jammed up there in Minneapolis so much and played by himself, with just piano and drums...
Oh, tell us about that, by the way, before you finish the other story. When was he up in Minneapolis?
So in 1930 and 1931 he was up in Minnesota, and he told you later on that he used to play with...
Frank Hines. He said he'd get to playing, and said sometimes he'd just play, and everything he played, he played it different.
Phillips - 189
Did he say something about a hundred choruses?
Yeah, he said he could play a hundred choruses and play them different.
So that was Frank Hines. And who else was with him then?
I don't know who else was in the band.
You mentioned something about him playing alone.
Yeah, he was playing, and there wasn't no other horn in there but him. Just he and the rhythm. They had drums and a bass, I think. Just about three or four of them.
So in '30 and '31, he got a lot of chance to spread out.

Yeah, he was playing by himself. He said, if you play by yourself, you can do that, because different ideas come to you, because you still don't want to be playing the same thing. That's what he said, the way he did it. He said he would think of other things to play. You know what I mean?
Did you notice if his playing changed before and after he was at that particular gig with Frank Hines? Did you notice any improvement?
Yeah. When he was with the Blue Devils. See, he was playing a whole lot more horn. He was playing a whole lot of horn when we met up with him in Oklahoma City.
And had that jam session up in your room.
Yeah. He was playing... He said he
Phillips - 190
stretched out on his horn, and he had to play by himself, and he said, "You know how it is playing by yourself; you got to play!"
That's interesting. You said he didn't practice alone, himself. But on the other hand, when he had this gig with Hines, he got a lot of chance to stretch out, and that helped his playing.
And he said that's why he practiced on gigs like that. That's the way he practiced.
Do you know any other gigs where he had a long chance to stretch out alone like that?

Yeah. Down at the Subway in Kansas City. Because wasn't nobody playing but him down there, until all the cats came in. Everybody would come in after the job was over. But see, he'd been there ever since round about 9 o'clock. They started coming in about 1 or 2 o'clock.
So that helped his vocabulary a bit.
Yeah.
That improved him.
